     6	## History of Vaccine Development
     7	
     8	The first vaccine was created by Edward Jenner in 1796 against smallpox, using cowpox to trigger immunity. It took nearly a century before the next vaccine (rabies) was developed, because scientists didn't yet understand germ theory. Once Louis Pasteur and Robert Koch established germ theory in the late 19th century, vaccines for rabies, cholera, and anthrax followed.
     9	
    10	The timeline from pathogen identification to vaccine licensure has shortened dramatically over the past 140 years:
    11	
    12	| Disease | Pathogen Identified | Vaccine Licensed | Gap (Years) |
    13	|---|---|---|---|
    14	| Typhoid fever | 1884 | 1989 | 105 |
    15	| Meningitis | 1889 | 1981 | 92 |
    16	| Whooping cough | 1906 | 1948 | 42 |
    17	| Polio | 1908 | 1955 | 47 |
    18	| Measles | 1953 | 1963 | 10 |
    19	| Chickenpox | 1953 | 1995 | 42 |
    20	| Hepatitis B | 1965 | 1981 | 16 |
    21	| Ebola | 1976 | 2019 | 43 |
    22	| COVID-19 | 2020 | 2020 | <1 |
    23	
    24	![Vaccination innovation timeline from 1880 to 2020](./assets/figure_3.jpg)
    25	
    26	Modern tools — advanced microscopy, genome sequencing, mRNA technology, and virus-like particles — have enabled faster and more precise vaccine design.
    27	
    28	## Dramatic Disease Reductions in the United States
    29	
    30	Data from Roush and Murphy (2007) shows the reduction in cases and deaths for vaccine-preventable diseases in the US after vaccine introduction. Several diseases achieved 100% elimination of both cases and deaths.
    31	
    32	| Disease | Pre-Vaccine Cases (per million/yr) | Post-Vaccine Cases (per million/yr) | Case Reduction | Pre-Vaccine Deaths (per million/yr) | Death Reduction |
    33	|---|---|---|---|---|---|
    34	| Diphtheria | 158 | 0 | 100% | 13.7 | 100% |
    35	| Measles | 3,044 | 0.2 | 99.99% | 2.5 | 100% |
    36	| Smallpox | 250 | 0 | 100% | 2.9 | 100% |
    37	| Acute polio | 141 | 0 | 100% | 10 | 100% |
    38	| Pertussis | 1,534 | 52 | 96.6% | 30.8 | 99.7% |
    39	| Rubella | 242 | 0.04 | 99.98% | 0.09 | 100% |
    40	| Hepatitis A | 465 | 51 | 89% | 0.5 | 88.7% |
    41	| Acute hepatitis B | 273 | 44 | 83.9% | 1 | 83.6% |
    42	| Pneumococcal | 233 | 139 | 40.5% | 24 | 31.3% |
    43	
    44	![US vaccine-preventable disease reductions](./assets/figure_1.jpg)
    45	
    46	## Measles Elimination Across US States
    47	
    48	A heatmap of measles cases per 100,000 across all 50 US states from 1929 to 2022 shows the dramatic impact of vaccination. Three key milestones transformed the landscape:
    49	
    50	- **1963**: First measles vaccine developed by John Enders
    51	- **1971**: MMR (measles-mumps-rubella) vaccine developed by Maurice Hilleman
    52	- **1980**: Vaccination became mandatory for children entering kindergarten
    53	
    54	Before 1963, nearly every state experienced high measles incidence (100–1,000+ cases per 100,000). After the 1980 mandate, cases dropped to near zero across all states, with only sporadic outbreaks.
    55	
    56	![Measles heatmap across US states](./assets/figure_2.jpg)
    57	
    58	## Smallpox Eradication: The Greatest Vaccination Success
    59	
    60	Smallpox was declared eradicated worldwide in 1980 — the only human disease to be fully eliminated through vaccination. Key factors enabling eradication: the virus infected only humans, symptoms were distinguishable, and the vaccine was cheap and effective. The WHO passed a resolution to eradicate smallpox in 1959, launched an intensified campaign in 1967, and the last natural case occurred in Somalia in 1977.
    61	
    62	## Herd Immunity and Remaining Challenges
    63	
    64	Vaccines protect not only individuals but entire communities through herd immunity. When enough people are vaccinated, pathogens cannot spread effectively, shielding those who cannot be vaccinated — newborns, immunocompromised individuals, and cancer patients on chemotherapy.
    65	
    66	However, significant challenges remain. Pneumococcal disease has seen only a 40.5% reduction in cases and 31.3% in deaths. Hepatitis A and B still show incomplete control. Globally, not everyone has access to vaccines, supply shortages put children at risk, and poor scientific understanding can reduce trust and uptake.
    67	
    68	## Key Findings
    69	
    70	- **Vaccines achieved 100% elimination** of cases and deaths for diphtheria, smallpox, and both forms of polio in the US.
    71	- **Vaccine development timelines have collapsed** from over 100 years (typhoid) to under 1 year (COVID-19), driven by mRNA technology and genomic tools.
    72	- **Measles cases dropped to near zero** across all 50 US states following the 1980 kindergarten vaccination mandate.
    73	- **Smallpox remains the only human disease eradicated** through vaccination, certified in 1980 after a global campaign.
    74	- **Gaps persist** for pneumococcal disease (40.5% case reduction), hepatitis A (89%), and hepatitis B (83.9%), highlighting the need for improved access, coverage, and newer vaccines.

    52	# PPTX Manipulation Skill
    53	
    54	## Overview
    55	
    56	This skill enables programmatic creation, editing, and manipulation of Microsoft PowerPoint (.pptx) presentations using the **python-pptx** library. Create professional slides with text, shapes, images, charts, and tables without manual editing.
    57	
    58	## How to Use
    59	
    60	1. Describe the presentation you want to create or modify
    61	2. Provide content, data, or images to include
    62	3. I'll generate python-pptx code and execute it
    63	
    64	**Example prompts:**
    65	- "Create a 10-slide pitch deck from this outline"
    66	- "Add a chart to slide 3 with this data"
    67	- "Extract all text from this presentation"
    68	- "Generate slides from this markdown content"

    72	### python-pptx Fundamentals

    75	from pptx import Presentation
    76	from pptx.util import Inches, Pt
    77	from pptx.enum.shapes import MSO_SHAPE
    78	from pptx.enum.text import PP_ALIGN
    79	
    80	# Create new presentation
    81	prs = Presentation()
    82	
    83	# Or open existing
    84	prs = Presentation('existing.pptx')
    85	```
    86	
    87	### Presentation Structure
    88	```
    89	Presentation
    90	├── slide_layouts (predefined layouts)
    91	├── slides (individual slides)
    92	│   ├── shapes (text, images, charts)
    93	│   │   ├── text_frame (paragraphs)
    94	│   │   └── table (rows, cells)
    95	│   └── placeholders (title, content)
    96	└── slide_masters (templates)
    97	```

   288	## Best Practices
   289	
   290	1. **Use Templates**: Start with a .pptx template for consistent branding
   291	2. **Layout First**: Plan slide structure before coding
   292	3. **Reuse Slide Masters**: Maintain consistency across presentations

   296	## Common Patterns

   298	### Slide Deck Generator
   299	```python
   300	def create_deck(title, slides_content):
   301	    prs = Presentation()
   302	    
   303	    # Title slide
   304	    slide = prs.slides.add_slide(prs.slide_layouts[0])
   305	    slide.shapes.title.text = title
   306	    
   307	    # Content slides
   308	    for slide_data in slides_content:
   309	        slide = prs.slides.add_slide(prs.slide_layouts[1])
   310	        slide.shapes.title.text = slide_data['title']
   311	        
   312	        body = slide.placeholders[1]
   313	        tf = body.text_frame
   314	        for i, point in enumerate(slide_data['points']):
   315	            if i == 0:
   316	                tf.text = point
   317	            else:
   318	                p = tf.add_paragraph()
   319	                p.text = point
   320	    
   321	    return prs
   322	```

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""
Build an 8-slide, 16:9 PowerPoint presentation:
"The Power of Vaccination: From Smallpox Eradication to COVID-19 in Record Time"
Data-forward, authoritative, accessible tone for public health professionals and policy analysts.
All data drawn directly from /app/benchmark/source_brief.md.
"""

from pptx import Presentation
from pptx.util import Inches, Pt, Emu
from pptx.enum.shapes import MSO_SHAPE
from pptx.enum.text import PP_ALIGN, MSO_ANCHOR
from pptx.enum.chart import XL_CHART_TYPE, XL_LEGEND_POSITION
from pptx.chart.data import CategoryChartData
from pptx.dml.color import RGBColor

# ── Constants ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
SLIDE_WIDTH = Inches(13.333)
SLIDE_HEIGHT = Inches(7.5)

# Color palette: deep teal / slate / clean accent
DARK_TEAL = RGBColor(0x0B, 0x4F, 0x6C)
ACCENT_ORANGE = RGBColor(0xE8, 0x5D, 0x04)
LIGHT_BG = RGBColor(0xF5, 0xF7, 0xFA)
WHITE = RGBColor(0xFF, 0xFF, 0xFF)
DARK_TEXT = RGBColor(0x1A, 0x20, 0x2C)
MEDIUM_TEXT = RGBColor(0x4A, 0x55, 0x66)
GREEN_OK = RGBColor(0x2E, 0x7D, 0x32)
RED_WARN = RGBColor(0xC6, 0x28, 0x28)
GRAY = RGBColor(0x90, 0x90, 0x90)

# ── Helpers ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
def set_slide_bg(slide, color):
    background = slide.background
    fill = background.fill
    fill.solid()
    fill.fore_color.rgb = color


def add_textbox(slide, left, top, width, height, text, font_size=Pt(14),
                bold=False, color=DARK_TEXT, align=PP_ALIGN.LEFT, font_name="Calibri"):
    box = slide.shapes.add_textbox(left, top, width, height)
    tf = box.text_frame
    tf.word_wrap = True
    p = tf.paragraphs[0]
    p.text = text
    p.font.size = font_size
    p.font.bold = bold
    p.font.color.rgb = color
    p.font.name = font_name
    p.alignment = align
    return box


def add_bullet_textbox(slide, left, top, width, height, bullets,
                       font_size=Pt(16), color=DARK_TEXT, font_name="Calibri"):
    box = slide.shapes.add_textbox(left, top, width, height)
    tf = box.text_frame
    tf.word_wrap = True
    for i, txt in enumerate(bullets):
        if i == 0:
            p = tf.paragraphs[0]
        else:
            p = tf.add_paragraph()
        p.text = txt
        p.font.size = font_size
        p.font.color.rgb = color
        p.font.name = font_name
        p.space_after = Pt(10)
    return box


# ── Presentation ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
prs = Presentation()
prs.slide_width = SLIDE_WIDTH
prs.slide_height = SLIDE_HEIGHT

# ═════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
# SLIDE 1: Title Slide
# ═════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
slide = prs.slides.add_slide(prs.slide_layouts[6])  # Blank
set_slide_bg(slide, DARK_TEAL)

# Title
title_box = add_textbox(slide, Inches(1), Inches(2.2), Inches(11.333), Inches(1.5),
                        "The Power of Vaccination: From Smallpox Eradication to COVID-19 in Record Time",
                        font_size=Pt(40), bold=True, color=WHITE, align=PP_ALIGN.CENTER)

# Subtitle
add_textbox(slide, Inches(1), Inches(3.8), Inches(11.333), Inches(0.8),
            "A data-driven overview of two centuries of vaccine innovation, disease elimination, and remaining gaps",
            font_size=Pt(20), bold=False, color=RGBColor(0xCC, 0xDD, 0xE5), align=PP_ALIGN.CENTER)

# Source attribution
add_textbox(slide, Inches(1), Inches(6.5), Inches(11.333), Inches(0.5),
            "Source: Our World in Data  |  Roush & Murphy (2007)",
            font_size=Pt(12), bold=False, color=RGBColor(0xAA, 0xBB, 0xCC), align=PP_ALIGN.CENTER)

# Decorative accent bar
accent = slide.shapes.add_shape(MSO_SHAPE.RECTANGLE, Inches(5.5), Inches(4.8), Inches(2.333), Inches(0.05))
accent.fill.solid()
accent.fill.fore_color.rgb = ACCENT_ORANGE
accent.line.fill.background()

# ═════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
# SLIDE 2: Vaccine Timeline Acceleration (horizontal bar chart)
# ═════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
slide = prs.slides.add_slide(prs.slide_layouts[6])
set_slide_bg(slide, LIGHT_BG)

add_textbox(slide, Inches(0.6), Inches(0.35), Inches(12), Inches(0.7),
            "From 100 Years to Under 1 Year: Vaccine Development Is Accelerating",
            font_size=Pt(28), bold=True, color=DARK_TEAL)

add_textbox(slide, Inches(0.6), Inches(0.95), Inches(12), Inches(0.4),
            "Time from pathogen identification to vaccine licensure, selected diseases (1884–2020)",
            font_size=Pt(14), bold=False, color=MEDIUM_TEXT)

# Horizontal bar chart data (diseases ordered by gap descending)
chart_data = CategoryChartData()
chart_data.categories = [
    "Typhoid fever (1884)",
    "Meningitis (1889)",
    "Ebola (1976)",
    "Chickenpox (1953)",
    "Whooping cough (1906)",
    "Polio (1908)",
    "Hepatitis B (1965)",
    "Measles (1953)",
    "COVID-19 (2020)",
]
chart_data.add_series("Years", (105, 92, 43, 42, 42, 47, 16, 10, 0.5))

x, y, cx, cy = Inches(0.6), Inches(1.5), Inches(9.5), Inches(5.2)
chart = slide.shapes.add_chart(XL_CHART_TYPE.BAR_CLUSTERED, x, y, cx, cy, chart_data).chart

chart.has_legend = False
chart.chart_title.text_frame.text = ""

# Style the bars
plot = chart.plots[0]
series = plot.series[0]
series.format.fill.solid()
series.format.fill.fore_color.rgb = DARK_TEAL

# Emphasize COVID-19 bar (last point) in orange
# python-pptx doesn't expose per-point fill easily via this API, but we can set the whole series;
# we'll add a visual callout instead.

# Axis formatting
category_axis = chart.category_axis
category_axis.tick_labels.font.size = Pt(11)
category_axis.tick_labels.font.name = "Calibri"

value_axis = chart.value_axis
value_axis.tick_labels.font.size = Pt(11)
value_axis.maximum_scale = 110
value_axis.minimum_scale = 0

# Callout box for COVID-19
add_textbox(slide, Inches(10.4), Inches(5.0), Inches(2.5), Inches(0.9),
            "COVID-19:\n<1 year\n(mRNA & genomic tools)",
            font_size=Pt(13), bold=True, color=ACCENT_ORANGE, align=PP_ALIGN.LEFT)

# Key insight box
insight = slide.shapes.add_shape(MSO_SHAPE.ROUNDED_RECTANGLE, Inches(10.4), Inches(1.8), Inches(2.5), Inches(2.6))
insight.fill.solid()
insight.fill.fore_color.rgb = WHITE
insight.line.color.rgb = DARK_TEAL
insight.line.width = Pt(1)
add_textbox(slide, Inches(10.5), Inches(1.9), Inches(2.3), Inches(2.4),
            "Key Insight\n\nEarly vaccines took decades because scientists didn't yet understand germ theory.\n\nModern tools — genome sequencing, mRNA, virus-like particles — collapsed timelines to months.",
            font_size=Pt(12), bold=False, color=DARK_TEXT)

# ═════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
# SLIDE 3: US Disease Elimination (structured table)
# ═════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
slide = prs.slides.add_slide(prs.slide_layouts[6])
set_slide_bg(slide, LIGHT_BG)

add_textbox(slide, Inches(0.5), Inches(0.3), Inches(12), Inches(0.7),
            "100% Case Reduction Achieved for Diphtheria, Polio, and Smallpox in the US",
            font_size=Pt(26), bold=True, color=DARK_TEAL)

add_textbox(slide, Inches(0.5), Inches(0.9), Inches(12), Inches(0.4),
            "Pre-vaccine vs. post-vaccine annual cases and deaths per million population (Roush & Murphy, 2007)",
            font_size=Pt(13), bold=False, color=MEDIUM_TEXT)

# Table: 10 rows (1 header + 9 data) x 6 cols
rows, cols = 10, 6
left = Inches(0.4)
top = Inches(1.4)
width = Inches(12.5)
height = Inches(5.5)
table = slide.shapes.add_table(rows, cols, left, top, width, height).table

table.columns[0].width = Inches(2.4)
table.columns[1].width = Inches(2.3)
table.columns[2].width = Inches(2.3)
table.columns[3].width = Inches(1.7)
table.columns[4].width = Inches(2.0)
table.columns[5].width = Inches(1.8)

headers = ["Disease", "Pre-Vaccine\nCases /M/yr", "Post-Vaccine\nCases /M/yr", "Case\nReduction", "Pre-Vaccine\nDeaths /M/yr", "Death\nReduction"]
for i, h in enumerate(headers):
    cell = table.cell(0, i)
    cell.text = h
    p = cell.text_frame.paragraphs[0]
    p.font.bold = True
    p.font.size = Pt(11)
    p.font.color.rgb = WHITE
    p.alignment = PP_ALIGN.CENTER
    cell.fill.solid()
    cell.fill.fore_color.rgb = DARK_TEAL

data = [
    ["Diphtheria", "158", "0", "100%", "13.7", "100%"],
    ["Measles", "3,044", "0.2", "99.99%", "2.5", "100%"],
    ["Smallpox", "250", "0", "100%", "2.9", "100%"],
    ["Acute polio", "141", "0", "100%", "10", "100%"],
    ["Pertussis", "1,534", "52", "96.6%", "30.8", "99.7%"],
    ["Rubella", "242", "0.04", "99.98%", "0.09", "100%"],
    ["Hepatitis A", "465", "51", "89%", "0.5", "88.7%"],
    ["Acute hepatitis B", "273", "44", "83.9%", "1", "83.6%"],
    ["Pneumococcal", "233", "139", "40.5%", "24", "31.3%"],
]

for r_idx, row in enumerate(data, 1):
    for c_idx, val in enumerate(row):
        cell = table.cell(r_idx, c_idx)
        cell.text = val
        p = cell.text_frame.paragraphs[0]
        p.font.size = Pt(11)
        p.font.name = "Calibri"
        p.alignment = PP_ALIGN.CENTER
        # Highlight 100% reductions in green
        if c_idx in (3, 5) and "100%" in val:
            p.font.color.rgb = GREEN_OK
            p.font.bold = True
        elif c_idx in (3, 5) and "%" in val:
            # Color-code lower reductions

                num = float(val.replace("%", ""))

        if r_idx % 2 == 0:

            font_size=Pt(11), bold=False, color=MEDIUM_TEXT)
